Priests cannot speak freely among themselves.
Laypeople cannot speak freely among themselves.
Priests cannot speak freely with laypeople.
Laypeople cannot speak freely with priests.
Secularized priests and secularized laypeople continue this habit for generations.
Polla ta deina—many are the terrible things.
Many terrible things I have seen.
Of many terrible things I have heard.
But the most terrible—but the most terrible—is and remains—nobody understands it;

nobody can grasp it: the most terrible thing is and remains the celibate bureaucracy that finds itself facing a reality—which it has itself helped create—in which Christianity is not even “Judaism for the people” anymore; and which now, in this admittedly precarious situation, looks around for new sources of strength—and of money.
This book by Peter Schneider has no form. It is a cancerous growth of extensive excerpts from a few of my writings, with my life’s work slobbered over by bland C. G. Jung ideas.
The book has no form because it has no fate. But not fate-less like Hölderlin’s sleeping infant. Fate-less like a Swiss man whose country has been neutral for more than a hundred years.
How was this author supposed to digest a life’s work such as mine? And how was he allowed to appear before the German public while suffering from such obvious digestive problems?

Meanwhile Hans Zehrer blows a tremendous trumpet blast into empty space by publishing an article on the permanent state of exception in Die Welt of 30 March 1957. It is a magnificent, though anonymous, German answer to the Swiss book’s complete lack of connection with reality. Zehrer dares to say openly that atomic power—which by its nature depends on secrecy—and democracy—which demands complete publicity—are incompatible.
Today, when a small sworn circle decides matters concerning the atom, we live under a permanent state of exception that more or less suspends democracy.
Faced with concrete realities like these, our Swiss ostrich prefers to stick his head into a bowl of whipped cream.

Behind my work on the state of exception lies the problem of the limits of what our modern, highly divided social machinery calls “law.” It is the problem of the limits of the courts and of judicial procedure.
The limit of what a modern legislator can turn into a statutory rule.
The limits of norms and normativity as such.
Naturally, asking about these limits brings one directly up against the territory of secrets and taboos.
As a young, inexperienced jurist, guided by no genuine teacher of constitutional or international law, I made a number of mistakes and violated more than one taboo.
That was serious and deserves correction. If Peter Schneider had asked and answered the question in that way, his book would have been magnificent, even if it had not been exhaustive.

Instead, as he calls it, he approaches the matter “anthropologically,” using a thin infusion of C. G. Jung’s categories, and asks about my personal secret—my Arcanum—on p. 96 of his book and elsewhere. And he ignores—with what right, exactly?—the passage in Ex Captivitate Salus, p. [75], where I formally deposited that Arcanum. He would have done better to consider my reference to the connection between dictatorship, sovereignty, and grace in the preface to Dictatorship, p. IX. And he should have remembered Rivarol’s warning not to betray the “perplexity of justice” and not to deal with problems “for which Themis has no scales.”
Peter Schneider’s book pushes me further into the problem of the judicial process itself:
Each of the three peoples that shaped European thought—the Greeks, the Romans, and the Jews—had one man who, for us Europeans, was their greatest.
Each of these three peoples killed its greatest man.
But only the people with the strongest sense of law and legal procedure—the Romans—did not kill their Julius Caesar judicially.

Queen Elizabeth of England sensed in 1585/86, through the instinct of royal blood, that it would have been less dangerous to the principle of monarchy to have Mary Stuart killed informally than to subject her to a formal trial before judges and an executioner appointed and authorized by Elizabeth herself.
She sensed the great precedent that would later lead to Cromwell’s trial and judicial killing of her successor Charles I in 1649.
And finally to the death blow against European monarchy: the judicial killing of Louis XVI by the Jacobins in 1793.
Compare J. E. Neale, Elizabeth and Her Parliaments 1584–1601, London, Jonathan Cape, 1957, pp. 140 ff.
The killing of Wallenstein in 1634, according to Pekař.
Under the impact of the judicial killing of Louis XVI, Kant wrote in his Doctrine of Right, Part II, General Remark, Meiner edition pp. 142 ff.:

“Even the murder of the monarch is not yet the worst thing—for one can still imagine that it was done out of fear—because it does not claim to be an act of punitive justice but an act of self-preservation.
It is the formal execution that fills a soul imbued with the rights of man with horror…”
The “complete overturning of all concepts of right”—Charles I, Louis XVI.
“That is the crimen mortale, inexpiabile—the mortal, unatonable crime—at bottom inexplicable because the criminal knowingly acts against the law,” and so on.
The reversal of the relationship between sovereign and people.
My opinion of 25 August 1945 on the scelus infandum—the unspeakable crime.

The country building socialism—that is, today’s Soviet Union—has used all its immense power for one purpose only: to bring power over human beings to an end! So says Ernst Bloch in The Principle of Hope, 1953, vol. 2, p. 490!!

All this so that “instead of the so-called constitutional state, which because of its rotten class content has become completely a state of injustice”—Ernst Bloch should never have touched this rickety contrast between Russia and the “state of injustice”; it is beneath him—so that, in the end, “no state at all will be necessary.” And in this way the monstrous super-state called the Soviet Union is justified!
Such faith I have found nowhere but in Israel!
Such justification by the final end I have not found even among the Jesuits!
In the spring of 1948 the famous atomic physicist Niels Bohr solemnly declared:
“Humanity will face decisive decisions five years from now. If by then it succeeds in avoiding war, the world will be saved.”
Those were his exact words. And he continued:
“By the end of those five years, natural science will have advanced so far that war will be impossible.”
At the end of those five years, natural science invented the hydrogen bomb.
That was the colossal advance that arrived.
This, and nothing else, is how natural science honors its predictions of progress and world peace.

To all these Nobel Prize winners who now warn us so impressively and lament so loudly—including the good, dear, brave Albert Schweitzer, who spoke so beautifully on the radio about radioactive radiation—to every one of these accusers and mourners I answer with Lucan’s lines from the Pharsalia IV.183–184:
Why beat your breast? Why, madman, do you groan? Why pour out useless tears, instead of admitting that of your own free will you obey the crime and fall into line the moment things become serious?
Lucan also gives us the most brilliant example of how a sense of law, in a situation of civil war, must lead to disaster—and all the more disastrously the better justified it is.
This is the story of Petreius. He stands on the just side, the side of the Senate, and warns against fraternization and betrayal (Pharsalia IV.212–235):
trahimur sub nomine pacis—we are being dragged along under the name of peace.
Everything can be applied to the present world situation.
The Roman is the man of law precisely because he knows the limits of law.
Everyone screams about Hitler’s violation of the principles of the constitutional state when he crushed the Röhm putsch.
Today they all scream in moral outrage: even the Reichswehr stained itself by taking part in Röhm’s murder.
Dachau trial, April/May 1957; Der Spiegel, no. 20, 15 May 1957.
So poor noble Röhm and the four million good SA men, infiltrated by Communists, were supposed to receive a proper constitutional-state trial—that is, a judicial trial!
How exactly are we supposed to imagine that in the situation of June 1934?
Would every single one of them presumably have had to receive a defense lawyer?
What these killers were capable of had been shown shortly before in the Potempa trial!
Is all this shouting about the constitutional state not grotesque if people seriously mean it as a description of what should have happened in 1934?
And if they do not seriously mean it for Röhm and the situation of 1934, and only use it to stir up general outrage, is it anything more than the lowest kind of preaching for a purpose?

Lucan’s knowledge of civil war remains simply admirable here too, as it does in the problem of Elizabeth and judicial procedure discussed above in the note of 28 April 1957. It is a sign of Victorian-aesthetic stupidity when Robert Graves tries to dismiss the magnificent Lucan as rhetorical cardboard kitsch. He is rhetorical. Thomas Hobbes already knew that and said so. But the rhetoric expresses his real situation.
The opposition between the rhetorical and the lyrical dominated the nineteenth century because politics had become fraud and ideology, while reality withdrew as truth into lyric poetry.
There, for one moment in Expressionism, it became politically explosive again.

Just listen to this line from Lucan about the informal murder of Pompey and compare it with Elizabeth’s occasional hope that someone would be found to murder Mary Stuart and spare her the trouble of legal proceedings.
Pompey’s murderer presents the victorious Caesar with the murdered Pompey’s head and says:
si scelus est plus te nobis debere fatere quod scelus hoc non ipse facis.
If this is a crime, then admit that you owe us all the more gratitude because we took it off your hands and you did not have to commit the crime yourself.
Hitler could have said that to the bourgeoisie in 1934 if he had possessed as much sense for law as he possessed for the situation.

But he was clever enough to hold on to legality instead and have the Reichstag give him a certificate clearing him by passing a law. He had boasted that at the time he had been the supreme judge of the nation. But to him that was merely a phrase. He would have found it extremely unpleasant if someone had taken him literally. That is what I naively tried to do in my essay “The Führer Protects the Law,” an essay whose boldness—indeed recklessness—nobody understood at the time.
